official_name: Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Parkinson's Disease
plain_title: Thinking changes that come with Parkinson's
one_liner: A decline in thinking that develops in a person who has had Parkinson's disease for a year or more.
in_simple_words: Parkinson's disease is best known for tremor, stiffness, and slowness, but it also affects thinking in many people over time. Mild changes, such as slower thinking, trouble multitasking, and finding words, are common. Some people develop dementia, usually years into the illness, with problems in attention, planning, and visual judgment, and sometimes hallucinations. It shares its biology with Lewy body dementia. Managing it well means balancing movement medicines with thinking, and supporting the whole person and family.
what_it_can_feel_like: Fifteen years of Parkinson's, and the slowness crept from his body into his thinking. The nurse specialist saw it before we did.
I can't do two things at once any more. One at a time, and I'm still me.
The Parkinson's helpline knew exactly what questions to ask about the hallucinations.
common_signs: Established Parkinson's disease for at least a year before thinking changes
Slowed thinking, trouble with attention, planning, and multitasking
Difficulty with visual judgment and finding the way
Visual hallucinations, apathy, anxiety, or depression

myths_vs_facts.fact: Thinking, mood, sleep, and bodily functions are all affected by Parkinson's. Cognitive change is common, especially later.
Many do over the long term, but many don't, and mild changes don't always progress.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Confusion means the Parkinson's medicines should be stopped.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Medicines need careful balancing, not stopping. A specialist can adjust them to protect both movement and thinking.

how_common.plain: Around 1 in 4 people with Parkinson's have mild thinking changes at diagnosis, and a majority develop dementia after many years with the disease.
how_common.figure: Mild NCD in about 27% of people with Parkinson's; dementia in up to 75% after 10 or more years (DSM-5-TR text and reviews)

what_helps.plain_summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, help thinking and hallucinations in Parkinson's dementia. Parkinson's medications are adjusted to balance movement and mental clarity. Antipsychotics are avoided or used very carefully, as in Lewy body dementia. Treating depression, sleep problems, and apathy helps. Occupational therapy, exercise, and cognitive strategies support daily life. Parkinson's nurse specialists and support organizations are invaluable.
evidence_based_options: Cholinesterase inhibitors, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Careful adjustment of Parkinson's medication by a specialist
Treatment of depression, sleep, and hallucinations with Parkinson's-safe approaches
Exercise, occupational therapy, and carer support
self_help_that_supports_care: One task at a time; written lists and routines
Exercise, which helps both movement and thinking
Reporting hallucinations or confusion early to the Parkinson's team
Parkinson's support groups and helplines for the person and family

when_to_reach_out: If someone with Parkinson's is becoming confused, slower in thinking, or seeing things, tell the Parkinson's team or doctor; medication adjustments and treatments can help. Sudden confusion may be an infection or medication problem and needs prompt assessment.
is_not: Slowness of movement and speech in Parkinson's can look like cognitive decline without being it. Depression and medication side effects cause similar changes. Lewy body dementia is diagnosed when thinking problems come first.
hope_note: Thinking changes in Parkinson's can be managed, and people continue to enjoy relationships, hobbies, and purpose with the right support.
